props.title: A Good Marriage

sections.content: Eric Rohmer's A Good Marriage (1982) stands as a pivotal entry in his "Comedies and Proverbs" series, following a headstrong young woman's methodical pursuit of matrimony. The film brilliantly subverts romantic comedy tropes while maintaining Rohmer's signature style of intellectual discourse and moral exploration. Like his earlier Claire's Knee (1970) and My Night at Maud's (1969), Rohmer crafts detailed character studies through extensive dialogue and subtle social observation.

sections.content: The film's protagonist Sabine represents a fascinating evolution in Rohmer's portrayal of young women, following the tradition of complex female characters like Chloe in Love in the Afternoon (1972) and Beatrice in Claire's Knee (1970). Her determined approach to finding a husband both satirizes and sympathizes with societal expectations of marriage, creating a nuanced commentary that feels remarkably contemporary despite its 1980s setting.

Within French New Wave cinema, A Good Marriage marked a significant shift from the movement's earlier experimental works like Godard's Breathless (1960) toward more structured narrative forms. Yet Rohmer maintains the movement's core interest in examining modern life and relationships with unflinching honesty, similar to Truffaut's later works like The Woman Next Door (1981). sections.content: The film's examination of marriage as both social institution and personal choice connects to a rich tradition in French cinema, from Jean Renoir's The Rules of the Game (1939) to Claude Chabrol's The Wedding Ring (1971). Rohmer's distinct approach favors moral ambiguity over clear judgment, letting viewers wrestle with Sabine's choices while understanding her motivations.
